domains.body:
**Qbḥt** ​— ‌Kebechet — ‌is ​the ​gentlest of ​the ​death-gods’ ​company: Anubis’ ‌daughter, ​who ​takes serpent ‌form ​and ‌brings the ​cool, ‌fresh ​water of ​purification ​to ​the dead. ​Where ‌her ​father ‌presides over ​the ‌weighing, ​she attends ‌to ​the ‌washing — ​the ​goddess ‌whose element, ‌water, ‌cleanses ​what the ​tomb ‌cannot.[^1]

### ​The Purifying ​Snake

‌In ​serpent form ​she ‌moves ​through ‌the embalming ​tent, ​her ​coolness the ​antidote ‌to ‌decay’s heat.

### ​Daughter ‌of ​Anubis

Child ​of ‌the ‌embalmer-god; she ‌extends ‌his ​craft from ‌wrapping ​to ​refreshing.

### The ​Cool ‌Water

​Her ​name means ​“cooling”; ‌the ​libation water ​she ​pours ‌revives the ​dead’s ‌senses.

### ​Guardian of ‌the ​Embalmers

‌Present at ‌every ​stage ​of the ​*wbt*-ritual: ​the ‌purification that ‌precedes ​mummification.

mythology.body:
Kebechet belongs ​to the small, ‌precise company of ‌Egyptian funerary deities ​whose work is ​a single gesture ​done perfectly. Her ​mythology is her ​function: the cooling ‌of the dead. ​In the Pyramid ​Texts she already ‌appears beside her ​father Anubis, refreshing ‌the king’s flesh ​with the ‌water that flows ​in the beyond’s ​own divine Nile.[^1]

### ​The Refresher of ​the King (Pyramid ​Texts)

The oldest ‌utterances name Kebechet ​among the court ‌of the embalming ​gods: she who ‌‘refreshes’ the king’s ​heart, whose cool ‌water runs in ​the celestial Nile. ‌The afterlife of ​the Pyramid Texts ​is a place ‌of thirsts quenched ‌— Kebechet is ‌the goddess holding ​the cup.[^2]

### The ​Washing Before the ‌Wrapping (Embalming Ritual)

​The mortuary liturgy ​divides into the ‌water-rites and the ​bandage-rites, and Kebechet ​presides over the ‌first. Before ​Anubis could wrap, ‌Kebechet had to ​cool — the ​purification that made ​the body fit ​to be eternal. ‌The ritual texts ‌address her directly ​as ‘ Kebechet ‌who is upon ​her father’s lake’.

### ​The Beneficent Snake ‌(Serpent Theology)

Egypt’s ‌serpent-goddesses divide between ‌the deadly (Meretseger, ‌the fiery Eye) ​and the beneficent; ‌Kebechet is the ​gentlest of the ​second company. Her ​serpent form is ‌coolness itself — ​the reptile of ​the water’s edge, ​at home in ‌the inundation’s margin ​where freshness collects.

### ​Her Father’s Lake ​(The Divine ‌Lake)

The embalming ​tent stood symbolically ‌at the edge ​of the sacred ‌lake where the ​gods washed; Kebechet ‌is its personification. ‌In vignettes of ​the judgement hall ​she appears beside ​the scales’ lake, ​ensuring the water ‌of the test ‌is cool, clean, ​and truthful.

overview.body:
**Kebehet** ​(*kebechet*) — ‌Purification, ‌the Cool ​Water of ​Offerings ​· The ​cooling ​water — ‌belongs to ​the ​Egyptian tradition, ‌where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Embalming, ​Purification". ​The name ​means "The ​cooling ​water"[^1].

**Qbḥt** ‌— ​Kebechet — ‌is ​the gentlest ‌of the ​death-gods’ ‌company: Anubis’ ​daughter, ‌who takes ​serpent form ​and ‌brings the ‌cool, ‌fresh water ​of purification ​to ‌the dead. ​Where ​her father ‌presides over ​the ​weighing, she ‌attends ​to the ‌washing ​— the ​goddess whose ​element, ​water, cleanses ‌what ‌the tomb ​cannot.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records ​the canonical ​scholarly ‌spelling **Kebehet** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ​[its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/kebechet/). The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*kebechet* contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Hieroglyphs ​as ​**𓈎𓃀𓎛𓏏**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"The cooling ‌water"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ‌**Kebehet** matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*kebechet* contains ​the ​same letters, ‌so ​no lost ‌diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ​is ‌claimed. The ​editorial ‌work is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed ‌reference spelling, ‌preserve ​capitalization and ​provenance, ‌and ​keep the ​original ‌evidence visible. ​The ​displayed form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description computed ​from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- **k** ​→ ​**K** — ‌Same, ‌capitalized
- **e** ‌→ ‌**e** ​— Same
- ‌**b** ​→ **b** ​— ​Same
- **e** ‌→ ​**e** — ​Same
- ​**c** → ‌**h** ​— ​Special phonetic ​character
- ‌**h** → ​**e** ‌— Special ​phonetic ‌character
- **e** ​→ ‌**t** — ‌Special ​phonetic ​character
- **t** ​→ ​**—** — ‌Dropped: ‌vowel not ​written
